explanation: The **nucleus** is the round body wrapped in a double nuclear membrane. The dark dot inside is the nucleolus. The nucleus holds the DNA, the coded instructions that control the cell's activities.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Tap the **large central vacuole**, the sac filled with cell sap.

image.alt: A plant cell with numbered markers on its parts

hint: It is the biggest structure in a mature plant cell, and it is full of watery fluid.
explanation: A mature plant cell usually has one **large central vacuole** surrounded by a single membrane and filled with **cell sap**. It stores water, minerals, sugars and wastes. By holding water it keeps the cell firm.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Tap the organelle where **photosynthesis** takes place.

image.alt: A plant cell with numbered markers on its parts

hint: It is green because it contains chlorophyll.
explanation: **Chloroplasts** are plastids that contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which absorbs sunlight. Inside, disc-shaped membranes holding chlorophyll sit in a fluid called the **stroma**. The sugars made are stored in the stroma along with starch granules.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Tap the **lysosome**, the clean-up system of this animal cell.

image.alt: An animal cell with numbered markers on its parts

hint: Look for a small, round, single-membrane sac packed with enzyme dots.
explanation: **Lysosomes** are single-membrane sacs filled with enzymes. They break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and even worn-out parts of the cell. The broken-down products can be reused by the cell.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Tap the **Golgi apparatus**, the cell's packaging and shipping centre.

image.alt: An animal cell with numbered markers on its parts

hint: It looks like a stack of flattened, curved sacs with small vesicles budding off.
explanation: The **Golgi apparatus** is a stack of flattened, sac-like structures. Like a post office, it modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles for transport, secretion or making lysosomes.

image.alt: A bacterial cell with numbered markers on its parts

hint: Look for the tangled thread in the middle of the cell.
explanation: In prokaryotic cells the DNA is a single circular molecule with no membrane around it. The region where it lies is called the **nucleoid**.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Tap the **cristae**, the folds that increase the surface area for energy production.

image.alt: A mitochondrion releasing ATP, with numbered markers

hint: They are finger-like folds of the inner membrane.
explanation: A mitochondrion has two membranes. The outer one is smooth and porous. The inner one is folded into finger-like **cristae**, which give more surface area for the reactions of cellular respiration. The energy released is stored as **ATP**.

explanation: The **nucleolus** is the dense round body in the nucleus where ribosomal subunits are made. The subunits leave through the **nuclear pores**, and one large plus one small subunit join in the cytoplasm to form a ribosome.

Ribosome

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Match each scientist with their discovery.

image.alt: Empty box-like compartments of cork seen under a microscope

right.text: A thread-like network in a barn owl's nerve cells (1898)
Any living plant cell can grow into a whole plant (1902)
New cells form only from pre-existing cells (1855)

hint: The picture shows what Hooke saw in a thin slice of cork.
explanation: **Hooke** (1665) saw box-like compartments in cork and called them cells. **Golgi** (1898) saw the network later named the Golgi apparatus. **Virchow** (1855) added that new cells come from pre-existing cells. **Haberlandt** (1902) proposed totipotency, the basis of plant tissue culture.

Animation of a cell swelling as water enters

prompt: Put these milestones on the road to the **Cell Theory** in time order.

image.alt: A compound light microscope

items.text: Virchow: new cells form only from pre-existing cells
Hooke: sees box-like 'cells' in cork
Schwann: all animals are made of cells
Schleiden: all plants are made of cells

explanation: **Hooke** observed cork cells in 1665. **Schleiden** reported in 1838 that all plants are made of cells, and **Schwann** in 1839 that all animals are. **Virchow** completed the Cell Theory in 1855: all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

prompt: You want to see dividing cells in an onion root tip. Arrange the steps in the correct order.

Water leaves by osmosis, so the contents shrink away from the rigid cell wall
Water enters the cell until it bursts
The cell wall dissolves in the sugar solution

It has large holes that let everything through
It is a liquid that fills the cell

explanation: The membrane is a **lipid bilayer** with proteins embedded in it. Its molecules can move sideways, flip and rotate, so it is **fluid**. The molecules are arranged like tiles, so it is a **mosaic**. It is only about 7–10 nm thick.

A rounded cell with a nucleus, mitochondria and other organelles but no wall

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Which of these is rich in **leucoplasts** that store starch?

image.alt: A green leaf
A ripe red tomato
A potato and a cut half showing white flesh
An orange marigold flower

hint: *Leukos* means white. Which one is white inside and full of stored food?
explanation: **Leucoplasts** are colourless plastids that store food such as starch, oils or proteins. Potato and taro cells store starch in them. Leaves are rich in **chloroplasts**, while tomatoes and marigolds owe their colour to **chromoplasts**.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Why is a ripe tomato **red**?

image.alt: A ripe red tomato

options.text: Its chloroplasts are full of chlorophyll
Its chromoplasts contain red, orange or yellow pigments

hint: *Chroma* means colour in Greek.
explanation: **Chromoplasts** are plastids with pigments other than chlorophyll, which can be yellow, orange or red. They colour flowers and fruits, attracting pollinators and the animals that disperse seeds.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: This plant has not been watered for days. Why does it droop?

image.alt: Animation of a potted plant wilting and recovering

options.text: Its chloroplasts stop working at once
Its vacuoles lose water, so the cells are no longer firm

hint: Which organelle stores large amounts of water and helps keep the cell firm?
explanation: The large central **vacuole** stores water and keeps pressure inside the cell, which makes the plant firm. Without enough water, vacuoles lose water, cells become less firm, and the plant **wilts**.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: The hot springs of Puga Valley in Ladakh stay close to boiling point. Which organisms mostly live in them?

image.alt: Animation of a steaming hot spring in a mountain valley, with rod-shaped bacteria magnified

hint: *Thermo* means heat and *phile* means lover.
explanation: **Thermophiles** are heat-loving, unicellular bacteria. Conditions in such hot springs may resemble the early Earth about 3.5 billion years ago. Scientists found that calcium carbonate forms rapidly there and may have protected early organic molecules.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: As an embryo's hand develops, the cells between the fingers die on schedule. What is this called?

image.alt: Animation of the webbing between an embryo's fingers disappearing

hint: The cell death is genetically planned.
explanation: **Programmed cell death** is a genetically regulated, organised way of removing selected cells. It is essential for normal development: without it we would have webbed hands. It also helps in quality control and immunity.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: A single plant cell, given nutrients and the right conditions, grows into a whole new plant. What is this ability called?

image.alt: Animation: a single plant cell becomes a cell mass and then a small plantlet

hint: Gottlieb Haberlandt proposed this idea in 1902.
explanation: **Totipotency** is the ability of a living plant cell, even a mature one, to develop into a complete plant. Haberlandt's idea laid the foundation of **plant tissue culture**.

subject: biology
chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: In 2010, Craig Venter's team put lab-made DNA into a bacterium whose own DNA had been removed. The cell grew and divided following the new DNA. What does this show?

image.alt: Animation: a bacterium's DNA is removed, synthetic DNA is added, and the cell divides

options.text: Scientists can build a complete living cell from non-living chemicals
DNA controls the structure and activities of a cell
The cytoplasm controls the cell, not the DNA
Bacteria do not need DNA to divide

hint: Only one part of the cell was made in the lab.
explanation: The cell followed the instructions of the inserted DNA, showing that **DNA controls the structure and activities of a cell**. Only the DNA was synthetic: the cytoplasm and membrane came from an existing living cell, so a complete cell was **not** made from scratch.

Mitochondrion
Vacuole

Rough endoplasmic reticulum

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Watch the animation of **mitosis**. Which statements are correct?

image.alt: Animation of one cell dividing into two identical cells

options.text: One parent cell forms two daughter cells
The daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent
It happens only in the testes and ovaries
Each daughter cell has the same number of chromosomes as the parent
It helps heal a cut on your skin

hint: One statement describes meiosis, not mitosis.
explanation: **Mitosis** makes two genetically identical daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent. It drives growth, repair (such as healing a cut) and asexual reproduction. Division only in testes and ovaries describes **meiosis**.

prompt: Which of these are **acellular** (not made of cells)?

explanation: **Viruses** (genetic material in a protein coat), **viroids** (genetic material with no protein coat) and **prions** (misfolded proteins with no genetic material) are acellular infectious agents. Bacteria and yeast are unicellular organisms.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.
